title: Filesystem behaviour

title: Evacuate /dev/sdd before removing it

explanation: sudo pvmove /dev/sdd mirrors every used extent onto the remaining PVs, online. After it finishes, vgreduce vg_lab /dev/sdd drops the now-empty disk, then pvremove wipes its LVM label.

title: Where do lv_logs's extents actually live?

title: Deactivate lv_logs temporarily

title: Add /dev/sde to vg_app

hint: Same shape as vgcreate — but it extends an existing VG.

explanation: sudo pvremove /dev/sdb zeroes the LVM metadata area. For leftover foreign signatures wipefs -a clears them all — then pvcreate can start fresh.

prompt: Show size and free space of vg_media only (not every VG on the system).
hint: vgs accepts VG names as arguments.
explanation: vgs vg_media filters the report to one group — VSize is its total extents, VFree the unallocated part.

title: Capacity planning
prompt: A 16G VG runs lv_data (5G), lv_logs (2G) and a 1G snapshot. How much VFree remains?
hint: Subtract every allocated volume, snapshot included.
explanation: 16 − 5 − 2 − 1 = 8G. Snapshots consume real extents — plan VFree for them, not just for LVs.

title: Resize lv_app to exactly 12G
prompt: Grow or shrink /dev/vg_lab/lv_app to an absolute size of 12G (not by a delta), resizing the filesystem too.
hint: Without the + sign, -L means an absolute size.
explanation: lvextend -L 12G -r sets the final size directly — no plus sign means absolute. lvresize handles both directions; lvreduce only shrinks (ext4 only — XFS cannot shrink).

title: Free-space math
prompt: A 10G VG holds lv_data at 4G and lv_logs at 2G. How much free space remains for new volumes?
explanation: 10G − 4G − 2G = 4G of VFree. vgs reports it directly — that is what lvcreate spends.

title: Activate every LV in vg_lab
prompt: Activate all logical volumes of vg_lab at once (after maintenance).
explanation: vgchange -ay vg_lab activates every LV in the group and recreates their device nodes — the classic post-recovery or post-import step.

title: Snapshot lv_logs before a risky deploy
prompt: Create a 512M snapshot of /dev/vg_lab/lv_logs named lv_logs_snap.
hint: lvcreate with the snapshot flag -s, sized with -L, based on the source volume.
explanation: lvcreate -s -n lv_logs_snap -L 512M vg_lab/lv_logs is nearly free — copy-on-write stores only blocks that change afterwards. Roll back with lvconvert --merge.

title: Remove the logical volume lv_db
prompt: Delete the logical volume /dev/vg_lab/lv_db (assume it is unmounted and no snapshot depends on it).
hint: lvremove, pointing at the full VG/LV path.
explanation: sudo lvremove /dev/vg_lab/lv_db returns its extents to the VG's free pool. lvremove asks for confirmation unless you pass -f. Data is gone instantly.

title: Wipe a disk clean of LVM
prompt: Erase the LVM label from /dev/sdd so it shows up as a plain empty disk again (assume it was already removed from any VG).
explanation: sudo pvremove /dev/sdd zeroes the LVM metadata area. For leftover foreign signatures wipefs -a clears them all — then pvcreate can start fresh.

title: Mount an LV via fstab
prompt: Write the /etc/fstab line that mounts /dev/vg_app/lv_logs at /mnt/logs with its ext4 filesystem at boot.
hint: device → mountpoint → fstype → options → dump → pass.
explanation: Use the stable /dev/vg_app/lv_logs symlink in fstab — it survives reboots because udev recreates it at activation.

title: Resize lv_data to exactly 8G
prompt: Grow or shrink /dev/vg_lab/lv_data to an absolute size of 8G (not by a delta), resizing the filesystem too.
hint: Without the + sign, -L means an absolute size.
explanation: lvextend -L 8G -r sets the final size directly — no plus sign means absolute. lvresize handles both directions; lvreduce only shrinks (ext4 only — XFS cannot shrink).

title: Grow lv_data by 4G — online
prompt: Grow /dev/vg_lab/lv_data by 4G AND resize the filesystem inside it, in one command, while the volume stays mounted.
hint: lvextend, plus the flag that also resizes the filesystem.
explanation: lvextend -L +4G -r grows the LV and the filesystem in one step — no unmount, no downtime. Without -r you'd run xfs_growfs (XFS) or resize2fs (ext4) separately.

title: Thin pools & advanced
prompt: Which command creates a thin pool named thin_pool of 10G in vg_lab?
options: The underlying pool can run out of physical blocks and start failing writes
Snapshots become impossible inside a thin pool
hint: Thin provisioning trades safety for flexibility — know both sides.
explanation: lvcreate -T builds a thin pool; thin LVs are then created from it with --thin or -V virtual sizes.

title: Carve a 2G logical volume
prompt: Create a logical volume named lv_logs with a size of 2G inside volume group vg_lab.
hint: lvcreate -n names it, -L sets the size, and the VG comes last.
explanation: sudo lvcreate -n lv_logs -L 2G vg_lab carves 2G of extents from vg_lab. The block device appears at /dev/vg_lab/lv_logs.

title: Plan the extents
prompt: You want a logical volume of exactly 3 GiB. How many 4 MiB extents will lvcreate consume?
explanation: 3 GiB → 3072 MiB ÷ 4 = 768 extents. lvextend -l accepts extent counts, -L accepts sizes — both land on the same result.

title: Deactivate lv_app temporarily
prompt: Deactivate the logical volume /dev/vg_lab/lv_app so its device node disappears (keep its metadata intact).
explanation: lvchange -an makes the kernel forget the device node until lvchange -ay reactivates it — useful before certain maintenance. Unmount first.

title: Snapshot mechanics
prompt: A 5G logical volume changes 200M of blocks after a snapshot. How much snapshot space is used?
options: Only the metadata, data is regenerated on merge
The origin volume is frozen until you delete the snapshot
Because LVM requires a snapshot before any write
About 200M — only changed blocks are stored
hint: Copy-on-write is proportional to churn, not to volume size.
explanation: COW stores just the overwritten old blocks: 200M changed ≈ 200M used. A 1G snapshot is plenty for a deploy window.

title: Name that command
prompt: Which command is used to add a PV to an existing volume group?
hint: It extends the group, not a volume.
explanation: vgextend is the right tool. Run the LVM commands with sudo, then verify with pvs/vgs/lvs.
practice: sudo pvs && sudo vgs && sudo lvs

title: Carve a 5G logical volume
prompt: Create a logical volume named lv_data with a size of 5G inside volume group vg_lab.
hint: lvcreate -n names it, -L sets the size, and the VG comes last.
explanation: sudo lvcreate -n lv_data -L 5G vg_lab carves 5G of extents from vg_lab. The block device appears at /dev/vg_lab/lv_data.

title: Operations deep-cuts
prompt: Which lvs field tells you an LV is currently active and open?
options: How many extents are free in the VG
Nothing — LVM hides failures by design
explanation: Attr — 'a' (active) plus 'o' (open) flags These details separate careful operators from lucky ones — vgexport/vgimport, Data% on snapshots, missing-PV handling and Attr flags.

title: Under the hood
prompt: Which pair of columns in pvs tells you a disk's contribution and remaining space?
options: Both grow and shrink — LVM pauses IO for both
hint: Think about what actually happens at the device-mapper level.
explanation: PSize is what the disk contributes to the VG; PFree is its unallocated part. 'Allocated 100%' means every extent is used.

title: VG size math
prompt: You pool three disks of 4G, 4G and 4G into one volume group. What is the VG's total size?
hint: A VG's size is simply the sum of its PVs.
explanation: vgcreate pools all PV space: three disks of 4G, 4G and 4G → 12G of extents (a tiny sliver goes to LVM metadata, invisible to vgs rounding). lvcreate spends that space.

title: Resize wisdom
prompt: Which flag pair extends an LV by exactly half of its current size?
options: df caches its results for 5 minutes
lvextend -l +50%FREE would need free space; -L +<half>G works regardless
hint: Percentages in -l refer to FREE space, not current size.
explanation: lvextend -l +50%FREE would need free space; -L +<half>G works regardless The LV and the filesystem are two different sizes — -r keeps them in sync; without it, run the grower yourself.

title: Evacuate /dev/nvme0n3 before removing it
prompt: Move every allocated extent off physical volume /dev/nvme0n3 so the disk can be removed from vg_data safely.
hint: One command relocates all used extents to the VG's other PVs.
explanation: sudo pvmove /dev/nvme0n3 mirrors every used extent onto the remaining PVs, online. After it finishes, vgreduce vg_data /dev/nvme0n3 drops the now-empty disk, then pvremove wipes its LVM label.

title: Name that command
prompt: Which command is used to drop an (empty) PV from a volume group?
hint: It reduces the VG's member disks.
explanation: vgreduce is the right tool. Run the LVM commands with sudo, then verify with pvs/vgs/lvs.
practice: sudo pvs && sudo vgs && sudo lvs

title: Thin pools & advanced
prompt: What is the main benefit of an LVM thin pool over classic (thick) LVs?
options: Thin volumes cannot be extended after creation
Thin volumes slow down by 50% when over half full
Volumes can be oversized beyond physical space — blocks are only consumed as written
hint: Thin provisioning trades safety for flexibility — know both sides.
explanation: Thin pools allocate blocks on first write, so a 100G thin LV costs nothing until used. Monitor the pool — overcommit cuts both ways.

title: Metadata & reporting
prompt: Which command restores a VG's metadata from a backup file?
explanation: vgcfgrestore -f /etc/lvm/backup/vg_lab vg_lab rebuilds the VG definition. Metadata loss is recoverable — data loss is not.

title: Capacity planning
prompt: A 24G VG runs lv_data (8G), lv_logs (2G) and a 1G snapshot. How much VFree remains?
hint: Subtract every allocated volume, snapshot included.
explanation: 24 − 8 − 2 − 1 = 13G. Snapshots consume real extents — plan VFree for them, not just for LVs.

title: Read the error
prompt: lvextend/lvcreate fails with: "Snapshot origin is busy / open". What is the actual problem?
options: Something is using the volume — unmount it (or stop the service) before merging
explanation: Something is using the volume — unmount it (or stop the service) before merging — LVM's error text is terse but precise. pvs/vgs/lvs tell you which of the numbers does not add up.
practice: sudo pvs && sudo vgs && sudo lvs

title: Report on one volume group
prompt: Show size and free space of vg_data only (not every VG on the system).
hint: vgs accepts VG names as arguments.
explanation: vgs vg_data filters the report to one group — VSize is its total extents, VFree the unallocated part.

title: Grow lv_data by 2G — online
prompt: Grow /dev/vg_lab/lv_data by 2G AND resize the filesystem inside it, in one command, while the volume stays mounted.
hint: lvextend, plus the flag that also resizes the filesystem.
explanation: lvextend -L +2G -r grows the LV and the filesystem in one step — no unmount, no downtime. Without -r you'd run xfs_growfs (XFS) or resize2fs (ext4) separately.

title: Thin pools & advanced
prompt: How do you watch a thin pool's real consumption?
options: lvs -a — the pool row's Data% shows how much of the pool is actually written
Snapshots become impossible inside a thin pool
hint: Thin provisioning trades safety for flexibility — know both sides.
explanation: Data% climbing towards 100% means the pool is filling; snapshot_autoextend-style monitoring or alerts should act on it.

title: Lifecycle & recovery
prompt: Which is the correct order to DESTROY an LVM stack completely?
options: Order does not matter — LVM figures it out
The PV must be brand new
hint: Remove from the top layer down.
explanation: umount → lvremove → vgremove → pvremove Destroy top-down, pvmove before vgreduce, and remember: /etc/lvm/backup holds METADATA only — data always needs a real backup.

title: Mount an LV via fstab
prompt: Write the /etc/fstab line that mounts /dev/vg_media/lv_app at /mnt/app with its ext4 filesystem at boot.
hint: device → mountpoint → fstype → options → dump → pass.
explanation: Use the stable /dev/vg_media/lv_app symlink in fstab — it survives reboots because udev recreates it at activation.

title: VG size math
prompt: You pool two disks of 10G and 2G into one volume group. What is the VG's total size?
hint: A VG's size is simply the sum of its PVs.
explanation: vgcreate pools all PV space: two disks of 10G and 2G → 12G of extents (a tiny sliver goes to LVM metadata, invisible to vgs rounding). lvcreate spends that space.

title: Rename a logical volume
prompt: Rename logical volume lv_test in vg_lab to lv_prod.
hint: lvrename takes VG, old name, new name.
explanation: lvrename only changes the name — size, data and filesystem are untouched. Update any fstab entries that pointed at the old path.

title: Spend the free pool
prompt: vgs shows 7G VFree. What is the largest single logical volume you can still create?
explanation: lvcreate can spend up to the whole VFree: 7G. In practice keep headroom for snapshots and future lvextends.

title: Plan the extents
prompt: You want a logical volume of exactly 2 GiB. How many 4 MiB extents will lvcreate consume?
explanation: 2 GiB → 2048 MiB ÷ 4 = 512 extents. lvextend -l accepts extent counts, -L accepts sizes — both land on the same result.

title: Three-layer model
prompt: What is an extent in LVM?
options: The VG's unit of allocation — 4 MiB by default
explanation: Extents (4 MiB by default) are LVM's currency: LVs are built from them and lvextend -l counts them, not bytes.
practice: sudo pvs && sudo vgs && sudo lvs

title: Resize wisdom
prompt: You extended the LV but df still shows the old size. What did you forget?
options: The filesystem resize — run xfs_growfs or lvextend -r next time
explanation: The filesystem resize — run xfs_growfs or lvextend -r next time The LV and the filesystem are two different sizes — -r keeps them in sync; without it, run the grower yourself.

title: Roll back with the snapshot
prompt: Merge the snapshot vg_lab/lv_media_snap back into its origin to undo everything since the snapshot.
hint: lvconvert has a --merge option that replays the snapshot into the origin.
explanation: lvconvert --merge vg_lab/lv_media_snap restores the origin to the exact snapshot state — in our lab we verified byte-identical content with sha256sum. Unmount the origin first if it's in use.

title: Evacuate /dev/sde before removing it
prompt: Move every allocated extent off physical volume /dev/sde so the disk can be removed from vg_app safely.
hint: One command relocates all used extents to the VG's other PVs.
explanation: sudo pvmove /dev/sde mirrors every used extent onto the remaining PVs, online. After it finishes, vgreduce vg_app /dev/sde drops the now-empty disk, then pvremove wipes its LVM label.

title: subtree_check
prompt: Which export style needs subtree_check the LEAST?
options: Exporting whole dedicated filesystems (their own mountpoint)
hint: Whole mounts have nothing to escape into.
explanation: Exporting whole dedicated filesystems (their own mountpoint) no_subtree_check trades a wall-off guarantee for stability under renames — export dedicated mounts and keep it off.

title: Verify your NFS mount is alive
prompt: Confirm from the client that 192.168.56.10:/srv/nfs/shared is mounted and show its filesystem stats.
hint: df on the mountpoint shows the NFS source.
explanation: df -h /mnt/shared lists 192.168.56.10:/srv/nfs/shared as the source. If the server is gone, a hard mount will hang here — that is the point of hard.

title: Performance & diagnostics
prompt: A server's nfsd threads are all busy. What symptom do clients see?
options: High response latency on every operation
explanation: High response latency on every operation nfsstat -c/-s, nfsiostat and /proc/net/rpc are the observability trio for NFS performance work.

title: Versions in practice
prompt: A legacy appliance only speaks v3. What must the firewall open?
options: v3 relies on NFS itself for locks
2049/tcp plus rpcbind 111 and the helper ports (mountd, statd, lockd)
The mount silently falls back to v3
explanation: 2049/tcp plus rpcbind 111 and the helper ports (mountd, statd, lockd) vers= pins the protocol; v4 integrated locking and sessions; v3 legacy means rpcbind + helper ports.

title: Composite mount options #5
prompt: Mount 192.168.1.50:/srv/share at /mnt/share with exactly these options: rw,async,no_root_squash (fast and dangerous — lab only).
hint: Options go after -o, comma-separated, before the device.
explanation: -o rw,async,no_root_squash — fast and dangerous — lab only. Read option lists as a sentence about failure behaviour; each word changes the risk profile.

title: Verify nia's group memberships
prompt: Print every group user nia belongs to (verify the team-share fix worked).
hint: groups or id, both take a username.
explanation: groups nia lists memberships; id nia also shows numeric uid/gids — the numbers that matter to NFS.

title: Options & limits
prompt: What does rsize/wsize tune?
options: The maximum bytes per READ/WRITE transfer — bigger helps throughput on fast networks
explanation: The maximum bytes per READ/WRITE transfer — bigger helps throughput on fast networks Effective access = export ∩ mount; rsize/wsize/actimeo are the perf dials; noexec/nosuid are hardening; v4 is TCP-only.

title: Declare an export for the 172.16.8.0/24 LAN
prompt: Append an /etc/exports line that shares /srv/nfs/home read-write with the 172.16.8.0/24 network, using sync and subtree_check.
hint: echo the line into /etc/exports with tee -a, or edit the file directly.
explanation: The exports line '/srv/nfs/home 172.16.8.0/24(rw,sync,subtree_check)' grants the 172.16.8.0/24 range read-write with synchronous writes. Then exportfs -ra applies it.

title: Who owns what
prompt: Which client-side credential decides a user's write access over NFS?
options: The numeric uid/gid of the user on the client
The client ran out of file descriptors
explanation: The numeric uid/gid of the user on the client NFS identity is numeric end-to-end: squash rules map uids, idmapd maps NAMES in v4, setgid keeps groups sane.

title: Open the NFSv4 firewall port
prompt: Allow NFS traffic from 192.168.56.0/24 through ufw — modern NFSv4 needs exactly one TCP port.
accepted: ufw allow from 192.168.56.0/24 to any port 2049 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow from 192.168.56.0/24 to any port 2049 proto tcp
explanation: NFSv4 needs just 2049/tcp — one rule instead of the v3 port parade (111, mountd, lockd, statd). Scope it to 192.168.56.0/24.
practice: sudo ufw allow from 192.168.56.0/24 to any port 2049 proto tcp

title: sync vs async
prompt: Which write mode do modern NFS servers default to when neither sync nor async is set?
options: It disables the network stack until writes finish
No default — the server refuses to start
There is nothing to verify — async is always fine
explanation: sync sync = ack after stable storage (safe); async = ack early (fast, risky on crash). Choose by what the data can afford to lose.

title: rpcbind & ports
prompt: You hardened the firewall to only 2049/tcp. Which protocol version still works?
options: NFSv4 — v3 needs rpcbind 111 and the helper ports
rpcbind is built into the kernel now
explanation: NFSv4 — v3 needs rpcbind 111 and the helper ports rpcbind = port 111 directory for v3 RPC services; v4 collapsed everything into 2049/tcp.

title: Probe 10.0.0.5's export list
prompt: From any client, list which directories 10.0.0.5 currently exports.
explanation: showmount -e 10.0.0.5 queries the server's mountd — the first diagnostic whenever a client mount is denied.

title: Caching & consistency
prompt: Why is NFS caching safe enough for most workloads?
options: Caching is unsafe for shared files
Clients validate cache freshness (actimeo) and flush on close — conflicts are rare and bounded
Clients poll the server once per second
explanation: Clients validate cache freshness (actimeo) and flush on close — conflicts are rare and bounded NFS consistency is close-to-open by default; noac/actimeo=0 trades speed for byte-exact freshness when a workload truly demands it.

title: What does the server export?
prompt: Ask the NFS server 192.168.56.10 which directories it exports, from a client machine.
hint: showmount queries the server's mount daemon.
explanation: showmount -e 192.168.56.10 lists exports + who may mount them. It is the first thing to check when a client mount is denied.

title: Hung mounts
prompt: What does the intr mount option do today?
options: It closes open files for you
Nothing — it is a deprecated no-op; signals to interrupted hard mounts are always allowed now
explanation: Nothing — it is a deprecated no-op; signals to interrupted hard mounts are always allowed now intr is history; processes can be signalled, umount -f/-l handle dead mounts, and soft mounts risk corruption on writes.

title: Open the NFSv4 firewall port
prompt: Allow NFS traffic from 10.0.0.0/8 through ufw — modern NFSv4 needs exactly one TCP port.
accepted: ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 2049 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 2049 proto tcp
explanation: NFSv4 needs just 2049/tcp — one rule instead of the v3 port parade (111, mountd, lockd, statd). Scope it to 10.0.0.0/8.
practice: sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 2049 proto tcp

title: Troubleshooting NFS
prompt: A client hits: "mount.nfs: Connection timed out". What is the most likely cause?
options: SELinux labels are wrong on the client
Port 2049/tcp is blocked by a firewall or the server IP is wrong
NFS is disabled in the kernel
explanation: Port 2049/tcp is blocked by a firewall or the server IP is wrong — triage order: showmount -e server (exports), ping/port 2049 (network), mount options (flags), then ownership (uid/gid).

title: Restart the NFS server cleanly
prompt: Restart the NFS server service so it re-reads its configuration.
hint: The Debian/Ubuntu service is called nfs-server.
explanation: sudo systemctl restart nfs-server reloads exports and daemons. For pure /etc/exports changes prefer exportfs -ra — no connection is dropped.

title: sync vs async
prompt: You see async on a production export. What is the FIRST thing to verify?
options: Whether the data on it can survive being partially lost — if not, move to sync
No default — the server refuses to start
async uses less CPU on clients
hint: Understand the failure mode before tuning.
explanation: Whether the data on it can survive being partially lost — if not, move to sync sync = ack after stable storage (safe); async = ack early (fast, risky on crash). Choose by what the data can afford to lose.

title: Mount the share on a client
prompt: Mount 192.168.1.50:/srv/share at /mnt/share with the NFS filesystem type.
explanation: sudo mount -t nfs 192.168.1.50:/srv/share /mnt/share attaches the remote share. Verify with df -h — it shows server:/path as the filesystem source.

title: Verify asha's group memberships
prompt: Print every group user asha belongs to (verify the team-share fix worked).
hint: groups or id, both take a username.
explanation: groups asha lists memberships; id asha also shows numeric uid/gids — the numbers that matter to NFS.

title: Verify lea's group memberships
prompt: Print every group user lea belongs to (verify the team-share fix worked).
hint: groups or id, both take a username.
explanation: groups lea lists memberships; id lea also shows numeric uid/gids — the numbers that matter to NFS.

title: Pin NFSv4 for the mount
prompt: Mount 192.168.56.10:/srv/nfs/shared at /mnt/shared forcing protocol version 4.1.
explanation: vers=4.1 refuses any negotiated downgrade — useful when you audit or benchmark a specific protocol version.

title: Shared-dir permissions
prompt: What does mode 2775 on a shared directory achieve?
options: Each user's files get their personal group — teammates hit permission denied
Only root can create files there
New files inherit the directory's group (setgid) while group stays writable
hint: The leading 2 is the setgid bit.
explanation: New files inherit the directory's group (setgid) while group stays writable setgid (2775) + consistent group membership across clients = a team share that just works.

title: Protocol internals
prompt: A client mounts server:/ and works under v4. What is it actually mounting?
options: The fsid=0 pseudo-root, with real exports bound beneath it
It force-mounts the export on boot
That subtrees are checked for viruses
explanation: The fsid=0 pseudo-root, with real exports bound beneath it v4's single-port design (2049) plus fsid=0 pseudo-roots replaced the v3 rpcbind port parade.

title: Protocol internals
prompt: Which daemon maps user names to ids for NFSv4 ownership strings?
options: It force-mounts the export on boot
It allocates the first free file handle
The physical root filesystem of the server
explanation: nfs-idmapd (idmapd) v4's single-port design (2049) plus fsid=0 pseudo-roots replaced the v3 rpcbind port parade.

title: Netgroups
prompt: What must the server resolve for netgroups to work?
options: The mount succeeds for root only
explanation: The netgroup definitions (via NIS/LDAP or /etc/netgroup) @netgroup specs centralise host access control; they resolve through NIS/LDAP — test with getent netgroup.

title: Check 192.168.56.10's RPC service table
prompt: Ask 192.168.56.10 which RPC program/port registrations it currently advertises.
explanation: rpcinfo -p 192.168.56.10 shows nfs on 2049 and mountd/lockd on their ports — the classic v3 connectivity sanity check.

title: Automation & tooling
prompt: What does nfsstat -s summarise?
options: A map file like /etc/auto.nfs referenced from auto.master
Inside the systemd unit file only
Server-side NFS operation counters (getattr, read, write…)
Per-mount RPC statistics — counts, latency and errors
explanation: Server-side NFS operation counters (getattr, read, write…) autofs for on-demand mounts; nfsstat/mountstats/nfsiostat for performance truth.

title: Netgroups
prompt: Which /etc/exports syntax grants access to the netgroup 'builders'?
explanation: /srv/nfs/shared @builders(rw,sync) @netgroup specs centralise host access control; they resolve through NIS/LDAP — test with getent netgroup.

title: Performance & diagnostics
prompt: Clients hang since a network blip. First diagnostic for a hard mount?
options: Check if the server answers on 2049 — the mount will recover when it does
explanation: Check if the server answers on 2049 — the mount will recover when it does nfsstat -c/-s, nfsiostat and /proc/net/rpc are the observability trio for NFS performance work.

title: Export syntax
prompt: Why can wildcard/CIDR client specs be risky?
options: They trust whatever the network says — a spoofed or new host inherits access
explanation: They trust whatever the network says — a spoofed or new host inherits access /etc/exports client specs: host, CIDR, wildcard, @netgroup — every broad spec widens who the server trusts.

title: Who owns what
prompt: Why does a file created via NFS show group 'team' instead of the creator's group?
options: A firewall rule dropped the mount port
The directory has setgid (2775) — new files inherit the directory's group
explanation: The directory has setgid (2775) — new files inherit the directory's group NFS identity is numeric end-to-end: squash rules map uids, idmapd maps NAMES in v4, setgid keeps groups sane.

title: Probe 192.168.56.10's export list
prompt: From any client, list which directories 192.168.56.10 currently exports.
explanation: showmount -e 192.168.56.10 queries the server's mountd — the first diagnostic whenever a client mount is denied.

title: autofs mechanics
prompt: Which master entry mounts every user's home from the server?
options: It needs one line per user in fstab
explanation: /home /etc/auto.home --timeout=60 (indirect map keyed by user) autofs = demand mounting with idle timeouts: direct maps for absolute paths, indirect maps keyed per user.

title: subtree_check
prompt: What is the performance cost of subtree_check?
options: Extra path validation on every file handle use
explanation: Extra path validation on every file handle use no_subtree_check trades a wall-off guarantee for stability under renames — export dedicated mounts and keep it off.

title: Inspecting mounts
prompt: Why prefer /proc/mounts over `mount` output in scripts?
options: It is the kernel's live table — no tool formatting surprises
explanation: It is the kernel's live table — no tool formatting surprises mount -t nfs,nfs4 for quick looks; /proc/mounts for truth; showmount -a for who is connected NOW.

explanation: docker diff proxy lists the writable layer's changes — A added, C changed, D deleted. Everything listed here dies with the container.

title: Run with --network host
prompt: Run image nginx:alpine detached as nettest-5 using the host network.
explanation: --network host: perfect for performance-critical proxies. Choose the smallest sandbox that works — default bridge for most, user-defined for DNS, host only when you mean it.

title: See what web changed on disk
prompt: Show the filesystem diff between container web and its image (added/changed/deleted files).
explanation: docker diff web lists the writable layer's changes — A added, C changed, D deleted. Everything listed here dies with the container.

title: Run with a named volume
prompt: Run container cache (any base image, e.g. ubuntu) with named volume redis_cache mounted at /data, detached.
explanation: -v redis_cache:/data creates/uses the named volume redis_cache. Volumes survive container removal — that is exactly what our lab demonstrates with docker rm.

title: Restart policy: no
prompt: Run image nginx:alpine detached as resilient with the restart policy no.
explanation: no (the default) never restarts — explicit non-policy for one-shot containers.

title: Cap a container's resources
prompt: Run image ubuntu detached as capped-1 with memory limited to 256m and CPUs limited to 0.5.
explanation: --memory 256m --cpus 0.5 hard-caps the cgroup limits. docker stats shows usage; exceeding memory gets the process OOM-killed.

title: Spot the live containers
prompt: Which command lists ONLY currently running containers, not stopped ones (variant 1)?
hint: The bare ps is filtered; -a widens it.
explanation: docker ps shows running containers; docker ps -a adds exited ones — muscle-memory both.

title: Port publishing
prompt: What is the safest default for a database container port?
options: Publish on 127.0.0.1 only (or not at all — use the docker network)
hint: Databases should not face the world.
explanation: Publish on 127.0.0.1 only (or not at all — use the docker network) EXPOSE documents, -p/-P publish. Loopback-only or network-internal access is the safe default for stateful services.

title: Inspect with a format filter
prompt: Print only the IP address of container web using docker inspect with a Go template.
hint: inspect -f takes a Go template over the JSON.
explanation: docker inspect -f '{{...}}' web extracts exact fields from the metadata JSON — scriptable, no manual JSON hunting.

title: Spot the live containers
prompt: Which command lists ONLY currently running containers (not stopped ones)?
hint: The bare ps is filtered; -a widens it.
explanation: docker ps shows running containers; docker ps -a adds stopped/exited ones. Variant 1 of this question — muscle-memory both.

title: Run with a named volume
prompt: Run container db (any base image, e.g. ubuntu) with named volume pg_data mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data, detached.
explanation: -v pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data creates/uses the named volume pg_data. Volumes survive container removal — that is exactly what our lab demonstrates with docker rm.

title: Save an image to a tarball
prompt: Export image redis:7 to the file image.tar so it can be moved to an air-gapped host.
hint: docker save writes a tar; docker load restores it.
explanation: docker save -o image.tar redis:7 packs all layers; on the other host docker load -i image.tar restores it. The offline alternative to a registry.

title: Recent logs with timestamps
prompt: Show container worker's logs from the last hour, each line stamped with its timestamp.
hint: --since bounds the range; -t/--timestamps adds the stamps.
explanation: docker logs --since 1h -t worker filters to the last hour with precise times — the fastest way to line a container up with a metrics spike.

options: always — and unless-stopped, except for ones you manually stopped
